content: An International Nonproprietary Name (INN), also referred to as a recommended International Nonproprietary Name (rINN), is the official generic or nonproprietary name assigned to a pharmaceutical substance. This designation is established by the World Health Organization (WHO). The existence of numerous proprietary or brand names for a single pharmaceutical substance can create confusion regarding the identity of the active ingredient. INNs address this issue by providing a standardized name for each substance, thereby facilitating clear and consistent communication. In the field of chemistry, a similar function is served by IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) names. However, IUPAC names are often lengthy and cumbersome, making them less practical for everyday use. INNs, on the other hand, are designed to be more user-friendly and accessible. The WHO issues INN names in multiple languages, including English, Latin, French, Russian, and Spanish. Although Arabic and Chinese were not part of the original naming scheme, these languages are now also included in the issuance of INN names. Drugs that belong to the same therapeutic or chemical class are typically assigned names that share a common stem. These stems are usually located at the end of the word (word-final), but in some cases, they may appear at the beginning of the word (word-initial). The collection of these stems is documented in a publication informally referred to as the Stem Book.
